The Guan Yu Shrine is a Chinese shrine on the hillside above Hua Thanon, just south of Lamai, crowned by a 16 m bronze statue of the Chinese general Guan Yu with a raised halberd. Entry is free, it is open daily from about 08:00 to 17:00, and a visit takes about 30 minutes. It is a working shrine and one of the focal points of Chinese New Year on Samui, which next falls on Saturday 6 February 2027.

Map and directions

The shrine sits on the inland (west) side of Route 4169 at Hua Thanon, about 4–5 km south of central Lamai. Coming from Lamai, look for a red gate on your right; the statue's red face and raised blade are visible from the road. The Hua Thanon fish market is about 300 m away on the seaward side.

Get directions: open the Guan Yu Shrine in Google Maps.

Who was Guan Yu?

Guan Yu was a real general of China's Three Kingdoms period, who served the warlord Liu Bei and died in 220 CE. Centuries of storytelling, above all the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, turned him into the model of loyalty, courage and keeping one's word. Over time he was deified. Taoists worship him as a god of war and protector against evil, Chinese Buddhists honour him as a guardian of the Dharma, and Confucians respect him as a model of righteousness.

In Thailand, where he is known as Guan U, he is especially popular with Thai-Chinese business owners, police and soldiers, who ask him for protection, honesty in dealings and success. You will recognise him anywhere by the same features: a red face (the colour of loyalty), a long black beard, green robes or armour, and the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, his long halberd.

The statue and the shrine

The bronze statue stands about 16 m tall on a raised base, taller than Big Buddha, and is described as the largest bronze statue of Guan Yu in Thailand. He is shown in dark-green and gold armour with a fierce red face, his beard flowing and his blade raised towards the sky. Scenes from his life are carved around the base. The shrine was built in the mid-2010s, organised by islanders of Chinese descent. The year usually given is 2014. [check]

Around the statue are a main shrine hall with altars to Guan Yu and other deities, smaller altars for offerings, red lanterns and plaques that compare Chinese and Thai religious traditions. From the upper level there are views over Hua Thanon's fishing boats and the sea.

Samui's Chinese heritage

Chinese traders, many from Hainan Island, settled on Samui generations ago and built the coconut and trading businesses that ran the island economy before tourism. Their descendants still keep shrines in Nathon (the Hainan shrine) and Maenam (San Chao Jao Eng Sae), and old wooden shophouses survive in Nathon and in a few streets near Hua Thanon. Hua Thanon itself is mainly a Muslim fishing community, with the island's central mosque, so in one small area you can see a Chinese shrine, a mosque and Buddhist temples within a few kilometres of each other. Read more in our history of Koh Samui.

Visiting the shrine: incense etiquette

  1. 1. Buy incense at the counter or stall; a small bundle costs a few dozen baht and goes to the shrine.
  2. 2. Light it from the flame provided, not from a candle on an altar. Wave it gently to put out any flame; never blow on incense.
  3. 3. Hold it with both hands at chest height, face the altar or statue, and bow three times.
  4. 4. Place it in the urn in front of the altar. If there are several urns, follow the order shown by signs or by local worshippers.
  5. 5. Offerings: fruit, flowers, tea and paper offerings are traditional. Don't offer beef at Chinese shrines.

General manners: cover shoulders and knees, don't point at the statues, keep voices low, don't climb on bases or railings, and give way to people praying. Photos of the statue and grounds are fine; ask before photographing worshippers. You may see the moon-block ritual, where two curved wooden blocks are dropped to get a "yes" or "no" from the deity; watch quietly rather than filming at close range. For Buddhist temple etiquette, see our Koh Samui temples guide.

Chinese New Year at the Guan Yu Shrine

Chinese New Year 2027 falls on Saturday 6 February 2027. Samui's celebrations spread over several days across three main places: Maenam's Chinese temple and Chinatown area (lion and dragon dances, the most family-friendly), the Hainan shrine in Nathon (the most traditional, which has included face-piercing rituals that may not suit children), and the Guan Yu Shrine at Hua Thanon. Expect red lanterns, incense, offerings, firecrackers and crowds of local families. The detailed 2027 programme is usually published in January, and we will add it to our Koh Samui Chinese New Year page. Chinese New Year is not an alcohol-ban day.

Best time to visit

Mornings are quieter and cooler, and the low sun lights the statue's face from the east. Midday is hot, with little shade on the upper level. The shrine is open all year. October to December is the north-east monsoon, with November the wettest month (about 445 mm), but showers usually pass quickly; February to April is the driest period. For atmosphere, come during Chinese New Year or the ninth-lunar-month vegetarian festival, when Chinese shrines across Thailand are busiest.

Parking, facilities and accessibility

  • Parking: drive through the red gate; there is parking for cars and scooters at the shrine. Pull out carefully onto Route 4169, which is fast and busy here.
  • Food: a seafood restaurant, Chomtalay, sits next to the shrine, and Hua Thanon has small local eateries, some serving Chinese-Hainanese dishes.
  • Facilities: basic toilets; offerings and incense on sale.
  • Accessibility: the site is on a hillside with steps between the levels. The lower courtyard and the view of the statue from below are manageable for most visitors; reaching the upper level means climbing.
  • With children: the statue impresses most kids, and the visit is short. Watch them near the incense urns, which are hot.

Samui Airport1625–30300–400500–700

Songthaews run past the shrine on the ring road during the day; locals pay about 30–80 THB (visitors are often asked 50–120 THB), cash only, and most stop by 20:00–22:00. Grab works from Lamai, but cars are fewer for the return; taxis don't use meters, so agree the fare first. On a scooter you need an International Driving Permit with the motorcycle category and a helmet (fine up to 2,000 THB). More in getting around Koh Samui.

Add a boat trip to your stay

Thong Krut pier, where Pig Island boats leave, is about 20–25 minutes from Hua Thanon. Ang Thong Marine Park is closed from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December.
